description: We are AYARU. Our mission is to make Earth science accessible to everyone by transforming NASA's Earth imagery and datasets into meaningful sounds. Led by Harsha Subash, a developer and innovator interested in web development, data visualization, and sound-based interfaces, we are building an interactive, accessible Earth Jukebox with real-time sonification, keyboard navigation, and live audio descriptions for blind, low-vision, and sound-based learners.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns NASA Earth imagery into sound, so people can hear changes on our planet as well as see them. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east. Each latitude band becomes a voice, pixel brightness controls loudness, and position controls pitch and stereo panning. Users can choose records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires. A year slider gradually detunes the sound to show the planet changing over time. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm and cool regions sound different. Users can also load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it instantly.

The project addresses the challenge by pairing EIC visuals with sonification generated in real time in the browser. It is also accessible, with keyboard controls, drag-to-scrub listening and a live text description of what is being heard. This matters because Earth science is mostly shared through images, which excludes blind and low-vision people. Sound makes climate data more inclusive and memorable for everyone.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns Earth imagery into sound, generated in real time in the browser. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east, like the planet turning under the sound. The map is split into 18 latitude bands, and each band is one voice. Pitch rises toward the north, brightness controls loudness, and longitude controls stereo position. A year slider (1980-2025) gradually detunes the voices, so the same record sounds more strained as the years pass. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm regions sound bright and cool regions sound mellow. Users can pick records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires, or load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it straight away. They can also record the mix. In a self-hosted version, the app can pull live imagery from NASA GIBS.

Benefits and intended impact

Earth science is mostly shared through images, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox gives them another way in, and it also helps anyone who learns well through sound. The intended impact is to make climate and Earth observation data inclusive, memorable and easy to explore, in classrooms, science outreach and public exhibits, without any installation.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no framework
  • Web Audio API for oscillators, filters, stereo panning and compression
  • Canvas for rendering the maps
  • MediaRecorder API for recording the audio
  • NASA GIBS imagery for the live-data version
  • [Add any AI tools, libraries or other software your team used. Space Apps asks teams to disclose AI use, so say how it was used.]

Creativity

The jukebox idea turns datasets into “records” you can pick and play, which makes data exploration feel like listening to music. Using the year slider to detune the sound lets people hear change over time, not just a snapshot. Mapping hue to timbre makes color audible too, and users can bring in their own frames.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, drag-to-hear listening and a live text caption that screen readers announce.
  • Simplicity: it runs in any modern browser, with no accounts or downloads.
  • Pleasant sound: each record uses its own musical scale so the sound is easy to listen to, not harsh.
  • Honesty about data: the built-in maps are illustrative, and real NASA imagery is loaded through the live version or by uploading a frame. The sound reflects the brightness and color of the rendered image, not raw measurements.
  • Future work: real EIC datasets, spoken summaries and a distinct sound for coastlines.
